summary.text: Take the admissible value \(n=51\), for which \(138n+6=7044\). Since \(2^{7044}\equiv670\pmod{1398}\), while \(2^{1398}\equiv1\pmod{1399}\) and \(2^{672}+3\equiv0\pmod{1399}\), the corresponding number is divisible by \(1399\), so its smallest prime factor is at most \(1399<1669\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(m)=2^{2^m+2}+3,
\]
so that \(a(m)\) is the smallest prime factor of \(A(m)\). We disprove the proposed statement by taking \(n=51\).

First observe that
\[
51\equiv 1\pmod 5,
\]
so \(51\not\equiv2\pmod5\), as required by the hypothesis of the conjecture. Moreover,
\[
138\cdot51+6=7038+6=7044.
\]
Thus the conjecture would imply
\[
a(7044)=1669.
\]
We will instead show that \(A(7044)\) has a divisor \(1399\). This forces its smallest prime factor to be at most \(1399<1669\), giving the contradiction.

We begin by reducing the exponent \(2^{7044}+2\) modulo \(1398\). Repeated squaring modulo \(1398\) gives the following table. In the row indexed by \(i\), the displayed residue is that of \(2^{2^i}\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
i&2^i&2^{2^i}\pmod{1398}\\ \hline
0&1&2\\
1&2&4\\
2&4&16\\
3&8&256\\
4&16&1228\\
5&32&940\\
6&64&64\\
7&128&1300\\
8&256&1216\\
9&512&970\\
10&1024&46\\
11&2048&718\\
12&4096&1060
\end{array}
\]
Each entry after the first is obtained by squaring the preceding entry and taking the remainder modulo \(1398\), so this is a direct finite modular computation.

The binary decomposition of \(7044\) is
\[
7044=4096+2048+512+256+128+4.
\]
Using the corresponding entries in the table, the successive products modulo \(1398\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{factors included}&\text{product modulo }1398\\ \hline
2^4&16\\
2^4,2^{128}&1228\\
2^4,2^{128},2^{256}&184\\
2^4,2^{128},2^{256},2^{512}&934\\
2^4,2^{128},2^{256},2^{512},2^{2048}&970\\
2^4,2^{128},2^{256},2^{512},2^{2048},2^{4096}&670.
\end{array}
\]
Consequently,
\[
2^{7044}\equiv670\pmod{1398},
\]
and hence
\[
2^{7044}+2\equiv672\pmod{1398}.
\]
Equivalently, there is a nonnegative integer \(k\) such that
\[
2^{7044}+2=1398k+672. \tag{1}
\]

We next perform the modular computations needed modulo \(1399\). Repeated squaring of \(2\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
i&2^i&2^{2^i}\pmod{1399}\\ \hline
0&1&2\\
1&2&4\\
2&4&16\\
3&8&256\\
4&16&1182\\
5&32&922\\
6&64&891\\
7&128&648\\
8&256&204\\
9&512&1045\\
10&1024&805.
\end{array}
\]
Again, every row follows by squaring the preceding residue modulo \(1399\).

Now
\[
1398=1024+256+64+32+16+4+2.
\]
Multiplying the table entries for these powers successively gives the residues
\[
4,\ 64,\ 102,\ 311,\ 99,\ 610,\ 1
\]
modulo \(1399\). Therefore
\[
2^{1398}\equiv1\pmod{1399}. \tag{2}
\]
Also,
\[
672=512+128+32.
\]
The relevant residues from the same table are
\[
2^{32}\equiv922,
\qquad 2^{128}\equiv648,
\qquad 2^{512}\equiv1045
\pmod{1399}.
\]
Their successive products are
\[
922\cdot648\equiv83\pmod{1399}
\]
and
\[
83\cdot1045\equiv1396\equiv-3\pmod{1399}.
\]
Thus
\[
2^{672}\equiv-3\pmod{1399}. \tag{3}
\]

Using equation (1) and the ordinary laws of exponents, we now obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(7044)
 &=2^{2^{7044}+2}+3\\
 &=2^{1398k+672}+3\\
 &=(2^{1398})^k2^{672}+3.
\end{aligned}
\]
Reducing this expression modulo \(1399\), equations (2) and (3) give
\[
A(7044)\equiv1^k(-3)+3\equiv0\pmod{1399}.
\]
Therefore
\[
1399\mid A(7044).
\]

For completeness, if a positive integer \(N>1\) has a divisor \(d>1\), then its smallest prime factor is at most \(d\): choose any prime factor \(q\) of \(d\); because \(d\mid N\), one has \(q\mid N\), and the smallest prime factor of \(N\) is at most \(q\le d\). Applying this to \(N=A(7044)\) and \(d=1399\) yields
\[
a(7044)\le1399.
\]
Since
\[
1399<1669,
\]
it follows that
\[
a(7044)\ne1669.
\]

But \(7044=138\cdot51+6\) and \(51\not\equiv2\pmod5\). Hence \(n=51\) satisfies the conjecture's side condition while its claimed conclusion fails. Therefore the assertion that, for every \(n\ge0\) with \(n\not\equiv2\pmod5\), one has \(a(138n+6)=1669\), is false.
